chapter_note.about: Concurrency control lets many transactions run at once while the result still looks as if they ran one after another. This chapter starts from the conflict test and the lock modes, then two-phase locking and its variants, deadlock, and finally the other big family, timestamp ordering with Thomas' write rule. Most questions give you a short schedule or a few timestamps and ask what is allowed, who waits, or who is rolled back. The last card compares what each protocol guarantees.
chapter_note.simple: Many people share one set of tools and want to work at the same time. One way is locks: grab every tool you need, then give them back, and never take a new tool after giving one back. That keeps things fair but people can end up waiting on each other in a circle. Another way is queue numbers: everyone gets a number and anyone who arrives too late for a tool is sent back to start again with a new number. Nobody waits, so there is no circle. In exam words: lock modes, two-phase locking and variants, deadlock prevention, timestamp ordering and Thomas' write rule.

cards.title: Conflict test recap
cards.simple: Two friends can swap places in a queue without changing anything only if what they do does not affect each other. Two people just reading the same notice can swap freely. Someone writing and someone reading the same notice cannot, because who goes first changes what the reader sees. If you can slide the actions of different people around, using only harmless swaps, until each person's actions are together, then the schedule is as good as taking turns. In exam words: only read-read pairs (and pairs on different items) commute; if swaps reach a serial schedule, it is conflict serializable.
cards.idea: A schedule is **conflict serializable** if swapping adjacent **non-conflicting** operations can turn it into a serial schedule. Operations commute only when they are on different items, or both are reads. The precedence-graph test says the same thing with a cycle check.
cards.definition: Two operations of different transactions **conflict** if they access the same item and at least one is a write. Two schedules are **conflict equivalent** if they order every conflicting pair the same way. $S$ is conflict serializable iff it is conflict equivalent to a serial schedule, iff its precedence graph is acyclic.
cards.intuition_full: This card is a short bridge from the transactions chapter into locking. A locking protocol is a way to make sure that only schedules which could be unscrambled by safe swaps are ever produced. The swap picture explains why only conflicting pairs matter: two non-conflicting operations leave the database in the same state in either order, so their relative order is not part of the outcome. If swaps can gather each transaction's operations together, the result is a serial schedule. If conflicting pairs force a cycle of 'must come before' constraints, no sequence of safe swaps can reach a serial schedule.

examples.setup: Schedule $S$: $r_1(x)\ w_2(y)\ w_1(x)\ r_2(x)$. Use swaps of adjacent non-conflicting operations to see whether it is equivalent to a serial schedule.
steps: $S$ is $r_1(x),\ w_2(y),\ w_1(x),\ r_2(x)$. Two adjacent operations can be swapped only if they do not conflict. Check each neighbouring pair.
$(r_1(x), w_2(y))$: different items, can swap. $(w_2(y), w_1(x))$: different items, can swap. $(w_1(x), r_2(x))$: same item, different transactions, one write: **conflict**, cannot swap.
Swap $w_2(y)$ and $w_1(x)$. The schedule becomes $r_1(x),\ w_1(x),\ w_2(y),\ r_2(x)$.
All of $T_1$'s operations now come before all of $T_2$'s: the serial schedule $T_1\,T_2$. Swaps keep the outcome unchanged, so $S$ is conflict equivalent to it, hence conflict serializable.
examples.answer: $S$ is conflict equivalent to the serial schedule $T_1\,T_2$.

examples.setup: For two different transactions, which adjacent pairs can be swapped without changing the outcome? (1) $r_1(x), r_2(x)$ (2) $w_1(x), r_2(y)$ (3) $r_1(x), w_2(x)$ (4) $w_1(x), w_2(x)$.
steps: A pair is swappable when its two operations commute: no conflict.

(2) Different items ($x$ and $y$): swappable.

examples.answer: Swappable: (1) and (2).

examples.setup: Schedule $S$: $r_1(x)\ w_2(x)\ w_1(x)$. Can swaps of non-conflicting neighbours turn it into a serial schedule?
steps: Neighbours: $(r_1(x), w_2(x))$ conflict, and $(w_2(x), w_1(x))$ conflict. Nothing can be swapped.
A serial schedule needs all of $T_1$ first ($r_1(x), w_1(x)$) or all of $T_2$ first. Neither is reachable without swapping a conflicting pair.
The precedence graph has $T_1 \to T_2$ (from $r_1, w_2$) and $T_2 \to T_1$ (from $w_2, w_1$): a cycle.
examples.answer: No. $S$ is not conflict serializable.

cards.title: Lock modes
cards.simple: Think of a library book. Many people can read the same book in the reading room at once. But if one person wants to write notes in it, nobody else may read or write it at that time. A shared lock is permission to read together with others. An exclusive lock is sole permission to read and write. A request that clashes with what is already held has to wait in the queue. In exam words: S (shared) is compatible only with S; X (exclusive) is compatible with nothing.
cards.idea: A **lock** is permission to use an item. A **shared (S)** lock allows reading and can be held by many transactions at once. An **exclusive (X)** lock allows writing and is held by only one. A request that is incompatible with the locks already held has to **wait**.
cards.definition:
Compatibility matrix (held vs requested): S/S yes, S/X no, X/S no, X/X no.

A transaction must hold $S$ (or $X$) to read and $X$ to write. **Upgrade:** converting $S$ to $X$ needs all other locks on the item to be released first. **Downgrade:** the reverse.
cards.intuition_full: The matrix mirrors the conflict rule from the transactions chapter: two operations conflict unless both are reads. Two shared locks are allowed together because two reads never conflict. Everything else would let a write overlap with another access, so it is refused. A lock manager keeps, for each item, the list of holders and a queue of waiters. Requests are granted in order when compatible. Upgrades are risky: if two transactions each hold a shared lock and both ask for an upgrade, each waits for the other. That is why some systems provide an update lock for 'read now, write later'.

examples.setup: Four transactions use item $A$. $T_1$ asks for a shared lock S, then $T_2$ asks for S, then $T_3$ asks for an exclusive lock X, then $T_1$ and $T_2$ unlock, and finally $T_4$ asks for S. Follow the lock table.
steps: $A$ is free. $T_1$ requests $S(A)$: granted. $A$ is held by $T_1$ in shared mode.
$T_2$ requests $S(A)$. Shared with shared is compatible, so it is granted. Many readers may share an item.
$T_3$ requests $X(A)$. Exclusive conflicts with the held shared locks, so $T_3$ must wait.
$T_1$ and $T_2$ unlock $A$. Now nothing is held, and the waiting $T_3$ is granted $X(A)$.
$T_4$ requests $S(A)$ while $T_3$ holds $X(A)$. Exclusive blocks everything, so $T_4$ waits.
examples.answer: Only S with S is compatible. $T_1$ and $T_2$ share; $T_3$ and then $T_4$ wait.

examples.setup: Current locks: $T_1$ holds $S(A)$ and $X(B)$; $T_2$ holds $S(C)$. Which new requests can be granted at once? (1) $T_3$: $S(A)$ (2) $T_3$: $X(A)$ (3) $T_3$: $S(B)$ (4) $T_4$: $X(C)$ (5) $T_4$: $S(C)$.
steps: (1) $S$ requested, $S$ held by $T_1$: compatible. Granted.
(2) $X$ requested while $S$ is held: conflict. Wait.
(3) $S$ requested while $X$ is held on $B$: conflict. Wait.
(4) $X$ requested while $T_2$ holds $S(C)$: conflict. Wait.
(5) $S$ requested, $S$ held on $C$: compatible. Granted.
examples.answer: Granted: (1) and (5). The rest must wait.

examples.setup: $T_1$ and $T_2$ both hold $S(A)$. Each now tries to **upgrade** to $X(A)$. What happens?
steps: An upgrade needs every other lock on $A$ to be gone.
$T_1$ waits for $T_2$ to release its $S(A)$, and $T_2$ waits for $T_1$ to release its $S(A)$.
Neither will release before it commits. This is a **deadlock**.
One transaction must be rolled back. A common fix is to request $X$ from the start if a write is likely.
examples.answer: Deadlock; one of the two must abort.

cards.title: Two-phase locking
cards.simple: Think of borrowing tools for a job. The rule is: first pick up every tool you will need, and only then start putting tools back. Once you put one tool back, you may not pick up another. If every worker follows this rule, workers who need the same tool cannot get in each other's way, and the jobs can be put in order of when each one finished picking up tools. In exam words: in two-phase locking all locks are acquired before the first unlock; this guarantees conflict serializability, in the order of the lock points.
cards.idea: **Two-phase locking (2PL)** says a transaction first only acquires locks (growing phase), then only releases them (shrinking phase). Once it unlocks anything, it may not lock again. Every schedule 2PL produces is **conflict serializable**.
cards.definition:
A transaction is **two-phase** if no lock request follows its first unlock. The **lock point** is the moment it holds all its locks (end of the growing phase).

**Theorem:** a schedule of 2PL transactions is conflict serializable, and the serial order is the order of the lock points. 2PL does *not* guarantee freedom from deadlock or recoverability.
cards.intuition_full: If $T_i$ and $T_j$ conflict on an item, one of them holds the lock first and the other must wait until it is released. Because of the two-phase rule, the first one has already reached its lock point by the time it releases anything, so everything it needs is already locked. Hence every conflict edge points from the transaction with the earlier lock point to the later one. A cycle would need a transaction with an earlier lock point than itself, which is impossible. So the precedence graph is acyclic. The same argument shows why a deadlock can still happen: two transactions each hold something the other wants during their growing phases. And since locks may be released before commit, other transactions can read uncommitted data, so recoverability is not guaranteed.

examples.setup: A transaction runs: lock-S($a$), lock-X($b$), lock-S($c$), unlock($c$), unlock($a$), unlock($b$). Is it two-phase, and where is its lock point?
steps: **Two-phase rule:** all lock requests come before the first unlock. A growing phase, then a shrinking phase.
lock-S($a$): one lock held.
lock-X($b$) and lock-S($c$): the count grows to 3. No unlock has happened yet.
The moment the last lock is acquired is the **lock point**. Here it is after lock-S($c$), with 3 locks held.
unlock($c$) and unlock($a$): the shrinking phase begins. From now on the transaction may not take any new lock.
unlock($b$): all released. Every lock came before every unlock, so the transaction is two-phase.
examples.answer: Yes, it is two-phase; the lock point is after lock-S($c$).

$T_a$: the first unlock is unlock($p$), and lock-X($r$) comes after it. Not two-phase.
$T_b$: both locks come before the first unlock. Two-phase.
$T_c$: lock-S($v$) comes after unlock($u$). Not two-phase.

steps: Under 2PL, a transaction holds every lock it will ever need at its lock point.
Two conflicting transactions cannot both hold the lock at once, so the one with the earlier lock point finishes its use of the item first.
The equivalent serial order is the order of lock points: 7, 9, 12, which is $T_2, T_3, T_1$.

cards.title: 2PL variants
cards.simple: Basic two-phase locking is like returning tools whenever you are done. Strict is a stronger rule: any tool you wrote with must stay locked until your whole job is signed off, so no one uses a half-finished result. Rigorous holds every tool, even ones you only looked at, until sign-off. Conservative takes all the tools at the very start, or does not start. Each stricter version gives an extra safety. In exam words: strict holds X locks to commit (cascadeless), rigorous holds all locks to commit (serial order equals commit order), conservative takes all locks first (no deadlock).
cards.idea: The variants of 2PL differ in **when locks are released**. **Strict** holds exclusive locks until commit or abort. **Rigorous** holds all locks until the end. **Conservative** acquires all locks before the transaction starts. Each adds a guarantee to plain serializability.
cards.definition: **Basic 2PL:** conflict serializable only. **Strict 2PL:** holds X locks until commit/abort; schedules are strict (hence cascadeless and recoverable). **Rigorous 2PL:** holds all locks until commit/abort; serial order = commit order. **Conservative (static) 2PL:** locks all items before running; deadlock-free but needs the read/write set in advance.
cards.intuition_full: The problem with basic 2PL is that an exclusive lock can be released early, so another transaction may read an uncommitted value. If the writer then aborts, the reader must abort too (a cascade), and if the reader has already committed the schedule is not even recoverable. Strict 2PL fixes this by delaying the release of exclusive locks until the writer's fate is decided. Rigorous goes further and makes the order of commits equal the equivalent serial order, which is simple to reason about. Conservative 2PL tackles a different problem: deadlock. If a transaction either gets all its locks at once or none, it never waits while holding something, so a wait cycle cannot form. The cost is that the read and write sets must be known in advance and concurrency is reduced.

cards.title: Deadlock
cards.simple: Imagine three friends in a corridor. Asha holds a door key and needs Ravi's key; Ravi needs Meera's; Meera needs Asha's. Everyone is waiting for the next person, so no one can move. That is a deadlock. To find it, draw an arrow from each waiting person to the person they wait for, and look for a loop. To prevent it, give everyone an age and agree: when an old person meets a young one, either the young one steps back or the old one forces the young one out. In exam words: deadlock is a cycle in the wait-for graph; wait-die and wound-wait use timestamps to prevent cycles.
cards.idea: A **deadlock** is a group of transactions each waiting for a lock another holds, in a circle. The system can detect it by finding a **cycle in the wait-for graph**, or prevent it with timestamp rules: **wait-die** and **wound-wait**. Aborted transactions restart with their original timestamp.
cards.definition:
**Wait-for graph:** nodes are transactions, with an edge $T_i \to T_j$ if $T_i$ waits for a lock held by $T_j$. A deadlock exists iff there is a cycle.

**Wait-die:** if $TS(T_i) < TS(T_j)$ (requester older) then $T_i$ waits, else $T_i$ dies. **Wound-wait:** if requester is older, it wounds (aborts) the holder; else it waits. Recovery by detection: choose a victim on the cycle and abort it.
cards.intuition_full: A cycle in the wait-for graph means no transaction on it can ever proceed, because each needs the next one to release a lock first. Detection finds the cycle and breaks it by aborting a victim, usually the cheapest or youngest. Prevention avoids cycles altogether by ordering waits. In wait-die, an older transaction may wait for a younger one but never the reverse, so the edges all point from older to younger and cannot form a loop. In wound-wait, a younger transaction may wait for an older one and never the reverse; again all edges point the same way by age. In both, the restarted transaction keeps its original timestamp so that it eventually becomes the oldest and cannot starve.

examples.setup: $T_1$ holds $A$, $T_2$ holds $B$, $T_3$ holds $C$. Then $T_1$ requests $B$, $T_2$ requests $C$ and $T_3$ requests $A$. Draw the wait-for graph, find the deadlock and break it.
steps: Each transaction holds one lock: $T_1$ has $A$, $T_2$ has $B$, $T_3$ has $C$. Nobody waits yet.
$T_1$ requests $B$, held by $T_2$. $T_1$ waits for $T_2$: edge $T_1 \to T_2$.
$T_2$ requests $C$, held by $T_3$. Edge $T_2 \to T_3$.
$T_3$ requests $A$, held by $T_1$. Edge $T_3 \to T_1$. The edges form the cycle $T_1 \to T_2 \to T_3 \to T_1$. Each waits for the next: **deadlock**.
Abort one victim, say $T_3$. It releases $C$, so $T_2$ gets $C$ and can finish, then $T_1$ gets $B$. The cycle is gone.
examples.answer: Deadlock cycle $T_1 \to T_2 \to T_3 \to T_1$; aborting any one of them breaks it.

examples.setup: $TS(T_1)=8$ and $TS(T_2)=3$ (a smaller timestamp is older). Apply wait-die and wound-wait to: (a) $T_1$ requests a lock held by $T_2$; (b) $T_2$ requests a lock held by $T_1$.
steps: **Wait-die** (non-preemptive): an older requester waits; a younger requester dies (is rolled back). **Wound-wait** (preemptive): an older requester wounds (aborts) the younger holder; a younger requester waits.
(a) $T_1$ (8, younger) asks $T_2$ (3, older). Wait-die: the younger requester dies, so $T_1$ is rolled back. Wound-wait: the younger requester waits.
(b) $T_2$ (3, older) asks $T_1$ (8, younger). Wait-die: the older requester waits. Wound-wait: the older wounds the younger, so $T_1$ is rolled back.
In both schemes waits only go in one direction of age, so no cycle can form.

With its **original** timestamp it keeps getting relatively older as others finish.
Eventually it is the oldest and never dies. So the restart keeps the original timestamp.

cards.title: Timestamp ordering
cards.simple: Imagine giving every student a number when they enter the exam hall, and the rule is that the work must look as if students took turns in the order of their numbers. Each item remembers the biggest number that has read it and the biggest number that has written it. If a student with a small number now tries to do something that a bigger-numbered student has already done, they have come too late and must start again with a new number. Nobody ever waits, so there is no deadlock. In exam words: basic timestamp ordering uses RTS and WTS; a late operation causes a rollback.
cards.idea: In **timestamp ordering** each transaction gets a timestamp when it starts. The protocol forces the equivalent serial order to be the timestamp order. Each item stores its largest reader and writer timestamps, $RTS$ and $WTS$. An operation that arrives too late is rejected, and its transaction **rolls back** and restarts with a new timestamp.
cards.definition:
**Read** $r_T(x)$: if $TS(T) < WTS(x)$, roll back $T$; else allow and set $RTS(x) = \max(RTS(x), TS(T))$.

**Write** $w_T(x)$: if $TS(T) < RTS(x)$ or $TS(T) < WTS(x)$, roll back $T$; else allow and set $WTS(x) = TS(T)$.

Guarantees: conflict serializable in timestamp order; deadlock-free; not necessarily recoverable or cascadeless.
cards.intuition_full: The serial order is decided up front by the timestamps, so any operation that would contradict it must be rejected. A read by an old transaction is too late if a younger transaction has already overwritten the value it should have seen: $TS < WTS$. A write is too late if a younger transaction has already read the old value, or already written a newer one: $TS < RTS$ or $TS < WTS$. Since transactions never wait, there is no wait-for graph and no deadlock. The cost is wasted work from rollbacks. Also, a transaction can read data written by an uncommitted younger writer's predecessor, so the basic protocol does not give recoverability.

steps: Rules. **Read** $r_T(x)$: if $TS(T) < WTS(x)$, roll $T$ back; else allow it and set $RTS(x)=\max(RTS(x), TS(T))$. **Write** $w_T(x)$: if $TS(T) < RTS(x)$ or $TS(T) < WTS(x)$, roll $T$ back; else allow it and set $WTS(x) = TS(T)$.

$w_3(x)$: $30 \ge RTS(x) = 20$ and $30 \ge WTS(x) = 0$. Allowed. $WTS(x) = 30$.
$r_1(x)$: $10 < WTS(x) = 30$. $T_1$ would read a value written by a younger transaction. **$T_1$ is rolled back.**
$w_2(x)$: $20 < WTS(x) = 30$. A younger transaction already wrote $x$. **$T_2$ is rolled back.**

cards.title: Thomas' write rule
cards.simple: Suppose you try to write a note on a page, but a later person has already written a newer note on the same page. Your note would be overwritten straight away, and nobody read it in between. So instead of throwing out your whole job, you simply skip that one note and carry on. But if someone later than you has already read the page, skipping would change what they saw, so you must still start again. In exam words: Thomas' write rule ignores an obsolete write instead of rolling back; it gives view serializable schedules.
cards.idea: In basic timestamp ordering, a write with $TS(T) < WTS(x)$ rolls $T$ back. **Thomas' write rule** says: if no later transaction has read $x$ ($TS(T) \ge RTS(x)$), just **skip** the obsolete write and let $T$ continue.
cards.definition:
**Write** $w_T(x)$ under Thomas' rule: if $TS(T) < RTS(x)$, roll back $T$. Else if $TS(T) < WTS(x)$, ignore the write (no rollback). Else perform it and set $WTS(x) = TS(T)$.

Reads follow the basic rule. The schedules are view serializable but not always conflict serializable.
cards.intuition_full: A write that is older than the current value can only matter to readers whose timestamps lie between it and the current writer. Those readers would have set $RTS(x)$ to at least their own timestamp. If $RTS(x) \le TS(T)$, no such reader exists, so the write would never be visible; the later write overwrites it. Skipping it saves a rollback and gives the same outcome as the serial order by timestamps. If $RTS(x) > TS(T)$, someone later has read the value that $T$'s write should have replaced, so that read would be wrong, and the rollback is necessary. That is why Thomas' rule produces view serializable schedules: the ignored write is a blind write whose effect is overwritten before any read.

cards.title: Protocol comparison
cards.simple: Four different traffic systems: one with waiting rooms where people can get stuck (basic 2PL), one that also forbids sharing half-finished work (strict 2PL), one that books everything before starting so no one gets stuck (conservative 2PL), and one that uses queue numbers and sends latecomers back to the start (timestamp ordering). All of them make the result look like people took turns. They differ in whether they can deadlock and whether a cancelled job can drag others down. In exam words: compare serializability, recoverability, cascadelessness and deadlock-freedom.
cards.idea: All the protocols here give **serializable** schedules. They differ in two more things: whether they can **deadlock**, and whether schedules are **recoverable** and **cascadeless**. Strict 2PL adds recoverability, conservative 2PL and timestamp ordering avoid deadlock, and Thomas' rule drops conflict to view serializability.
cards.definition:
**Summary table.**

| Protocol | CSR | Recoverable | Cascadeless | Deadlock-free |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Basic 2PL | yes | no | no | no |
| Strict 2PL | yes | yes | yes | no |
| Conservative 2PL | yes | no | no | yes |
| Timestamp ordering | yes | no | no | yes |
| TSO + Thomas | view only | no | no | yes |
cards.intuition_full: Locks and timestamps solve the same problem in opposite ways. Locks make a conflicting transaction wait, which risks a deadlock but wastes little work. Timestamps never wait, which means no deadlock, but conflicting transactions are rolled back and redone. Recoverability is a separate concern about commit order, and neither pure family gives it by itself. Strict 2PL gets it by holding exclusive locks to commit; timestamp ordering can be given it by delaying reads or commits (variants not in the syllabus). The sets of schedules accepted by 2PL and by timestamp ordering are incomparable: each accepts some schedules the other rejects.

examples.setup: Fill in what each protocol guarantees: conflict serializability (CSR), recoverability (Rec), cascadeless (ACA), and freedom from deadlock (No DL), for basic 2PL, strict 2PL, conservative 2PL, basic timestamp ordering and timestamp ordering with Thomas' rule.
steps: **Basic 2PL:** conflict serializable. It can release exclusive locks early, so no recoverability. It can deadlock.

**Conservative 2PL:** conflict serializable and deadlock-free (no hold-and-wait). Not recoverable by itself.
**Basic timestamp ordering:** conflict serializable in timestamp order and deadlock-free (no waiting). Not recoverable by itself.

examples.setup: Which statements are true? (a) Every schedule allowed by strict 2PL is cascadeless. (b) Every schedule allowed by basic timestamp ordering is recoverable. (c) 2PL can deadlock but timestamp ordering cannot. (d) Thomas' rule schedules are always conflict serializable. (e) Conservative 2PL is deadlock-free.
steps: (a) True: X locks held to commit prevents dirty reads.
(b) False: basic TSO lets a transaction read data written by an uncommitted writer and then commit first, so it is not recoverable by itself.
(c) True: 2PL waits for locks, TSO never waits.
(d) False: Thomas' rule gives view serializable schedules only.
(e) True: all locks are acquired at the start, so no hold-and-wait.
examples.answer: True: (a), (c), (e). False: (b), (d).

examples.setup: With $TS(T_1) < TS(T_2)$, is $S: r_1(x)\ w_2(x)\ r_1(y)$ allowed by timestamp ordering? By 2PL?
steps: Timestamp ordering: $r_1(x)$ sets $RTS(x) = TS(T_1)$. $w_2(x)$: $TS(T_2) \ge RTS(x)$, allowed. $r_1(y)$ is untouched. All allowed.
2PL: $T_2$ needs $X(x)$ after $r_1(x)$, so $T_1$ must have released $S(x)$ by then.
But $T_1$ still needs to lock $y$ afterwards. That is a lock after an unlock, which breaks the two-phase rule.
So this interleaving is possible under timestamp ordering and impossible under 2PL. The sets of schedules the two protocols accept are not nested.
examples.answer: Allowed by timestamp ordering; not producible by 2PL.

steps.caption: $S$ is $r_1(x),\ w_2(y),\ w_1(x),\ r_2(x)$. Two adjacent operations can be swapped only if they do not conflict. Check each neighbouring pair.
$(r_1(x), w_2(y))$: different items, can swap. $(w_2(y), w_1(x))$: different items, can swap. $(w_1(x), r_2(x))$: same item, different transactions, one write: **conflict**, cannot swap.
Swap $w_2(y)$ and $w_1(x)$. The schedule becomes $r_1(x),\ w_1(x),\ w_2(y),\ r_2(x)$.
All of $T_1$'s operations now come before all of $T_2$'s: the serial schedule $T_1\,T_2$. Swaps keep the outcome unchanged, so $S$ is conflict equivalent to it, hence conflict serializable.

scenes.title: Shared and exclusive locks on item A

steps.caption: $A$ is free. $T_1$ requests $S(A)$: granted. $A$ is held by $T_1$ in shared mode.
$T_2$ requests $S(A)$. Shared with shared is compatible, so it is granted. Many readers may share an item.
$T_3$ requests $X(A)$. Exclusive conflicts with the held shared locks, so $T_3$ must wait.

steps.caption: $T_1$ and $T_2$ unlock $A$. Now nothing is held, and the waiting $T_3$ is granted $X(A)$.

steps.caption: $T_4$ requests $S(A)$ while $T_3$ holds $X(A)$. Exclusive blocks everything, so $T_4$ waits.

scenes.title: Locks held over time: growing then shrinking

steps.caption: **Two-phase rule:** all lock requests come before the first unlock. A growing phase, then a shrinking phase.

set.text: all locks first, then all unlocks

steps.caption: lock-S($a$): one lock held.
lock-X($b$) and lock-S($c$): the count grows to 3. No unlock has happened yet.
The moment the last lock is acquired is the **lock point**. Here it is after lock-S($c$), with 3 locks held.
unlock($c$) and unlock($a$): the shrinking phase begins. From now on the transaction may not take any new lock.
unlock($b$): all released. Every lock came before every unlock, so the transaction is two-phase.

scenes.title: When each 2PL variant holds its locks

steps.caption: The transaction needs $S(a)$ from time 1 and $X(b)$ from time 2, and commits at time 6. Its lock point is time 2.
**Basic 2PL:** after the lock point, locks may be released at any time. Here $S(a)$ is released at 3 and $X(b)$ at 4, before the commit.
**Strict 2PL:** every exclusive lock is held until commit or abort. $X(b)$ is held to time 6; $S(a)$ may still be released early. No one can read dirty data, so schedules are cascadeless.
**Rigorous 2PL:** all locks, shared and exclusive, are held until commit. The serial order equals the commit order.
**Conservative 2PL:** acquire all locks before starting, at time 0, or wait. There is no waiting while holding locks, so no deadlock.

scenes.title: A wait-for cycle and breaking it

steps.caption: Each transaction holds one lock: $T_1$ has $A$, $T_2$ has $B$, $T_3$ has $C$. Nobody waits yet.
$T_1$ requests $B$, held by $T_2$. $T_1$ waits for $T_2$: edge $T_1 \to T_2$.
$T_2$ requests $C$, held by $T_3$. Edge $T_2 \to T_3$.
$T_3$ requests $A$, held by $T_1$. Edge $T_3 \to T_1$. The edges form the cycle $T_1 \to T_2 \to T_3 \to T_1$. Each waits for the next: **deadlock**.
Abort one victim, say $T_3$. It releases $C$, so $T_2$ gets $C$ and can finish, then $T_1$ gets $B$. The cycle is gone.
